Dirichlet's Theorem on Arithmetic Progressions. If you take two coprime positive integers called a and d, then the arithmetic progression a, a plus d, a plus two d, a plus three d, and so on, will contain infinitely many primes. This theorem was proved by Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet in 1837, and it generalizes Euclid's proof of the infinitude of primes to linear progressions. The result marked the birth of analytic number theory by introducing methods from analysis to solve algebraic questions. The coprimality requirement is crucial: if a and d shared a common divisor greater than one, every term in the progression would be a multiple of that divisor, leaving room for at most one prime. Consider the progression four n plus three, which yields 3, 7, 11, 19, 23, 31, and so on, containing infinitely many primes. To prove the theorem, Dirichlet introduced Dirichlet characters and Dirichlet L-functions, which are complex analytic generalizations of the Riemann zeta function. The proof demonstrates that the sum of the reciprocals of the primes in the progression diverges, showing that the primes not only exist in infinite quantity but also possess non-zero density. The theorem implies that primes are distributed asymptotically equally among the coprime residue classes modulo d, where the count of such classes is given by Euler's totient function. This result connects to the Riemann Hypothesis, which generalizes to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, and to a specialized variant of the Prime Number Theorem that quantifies prime distribution in these sequences.
